solution_full: At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $2\cos2x-1=2\cdot\dfrac12-1=0$, while $\tan3x$ is unbounded because $3x\to\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. The limit is of the form $0\cdot\infty$.

Double-angle formula: $4\cos^{2}x=2(1+\cos2x)$, so $4\cos^{2}x-3=2\cos2x-1$. Hence $\cos3x=\cos x\,(2\cos2x-1)$, that is, $2\cos2x-1=\dfrac{\cos3x}{\cos x}$ (valid because $\cos x\neq0$ near $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$).

This is continuous at $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so the limit is $\dfrac{\sin(\pi/2)}{\cos(\pi/6)}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}/2}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$. The cancelled factor $\cos3x$ changes sign at $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in both factors, so the left and right limits agree.
(A sign slip in L'Hopital's rule gives $-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$; using $\sin x$ in place of $\cos x$ in the denominator gives $2$.)
originality_note: New: the factor 2cos2x - 1 is exactly cos3x/cos x (triple angle written through the double angle), so the 0 times infinity product with tan3x collapses to sin3x/cos x (way 5). Closest known: lim (1 - tan x)(tan2x) type products resolved by the 2A formula. Different because: the vanishing factor is the double-angle form of the triple-angle identity, which must be recognised to cancel cos3x.
